total:
\(How much hardness do product distributions miss? At least a polynomial factor, and no upper bound of any kind is known.\) total Wide open #

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{R}(g_d) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{prod}}(g_d)^{1.08}\big)\)
    witness: \(\bar{\wedge}\text{-tree}\) Sanyal24
    The balanced NAND tree has $\mathrm{R} = \Theta(N^{0.75384\ldots})$ [Santha95] and $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{prod}} = O(N^{0.69789\ldots})$ [Sanyal24, Lem. 1.8], a ratio of exponents of $1.0802\ldots$. This is the first -- and so far only -- polynomial separation of the two.

The other direction is $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{prod}} \le \mathrm{R}$ by Yao, so the cell is asking how far a product distribution can be from optimal. Nothing polynomial is known: the best general statement in this direction runs through sabotage complexity, $\mathrm{RS} = \tilde\Omega(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{prod}})$, and that is a bound on $\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{prod}}$ from above, not below. It is also the wrong shape to close the cell even if \(\mathrm{RS}(f)\) were known to be $\Theta(\mathrm{R})$, which is itself the Ben-David-Kothari question at Is … for total …?.

Why the NAND tree separates is worth stating, because the natural guess is that it does not. Saks and Wigderson's $\Theta(\alpha^d)$ lower bound, $\alpha = (1+\sqrt{33})/4$, is proved against a product distribution -- but for zero-error cost. Allowing error $1/3$ lets an algorithm that knows $\mu$ recurse first on the child likelier to evaluate to $0$ instead of on a random one, and under a product distribution the two subtrees are independent, so that greedy choice is available at every level and compounds over the depth. Against a correlated distribution it is not.

\(\text{Solving } f^{\otimes k} \text{ with } \ll k\,\mathrm{R}(f) \text{ queries succeeds with probability } 2^{-\Omega(k)}\) total Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\text{Any } \gamma^3\mathrm{R}(f)k/11 \text{-query algorithm computes } f^{\otimes k} \text{ correctly with probability} < (1/2+\gamma)^k\)
    Drucker12
    Theorem 1.2, for Boolean $f$ and $0<\gamma<1/4$. It replaced the earlier bound of [KSdW07], whose query budget scaled as $\mathrm{bs}(f)k$ -- which can be as small as $\mathrm{R}(f)^{1/2}k$, since $\mathrm{R}(f)^{1/3} \le \mathrm{bs}(f) \le \mathrm{R}(f)$ and a power-$2$ separation is known. Proving a DPT at the $\mathrm{R}(f)k$ scale was one of the main open problems in classical query complexity.
  • \(\mathrm{Suc}_{T,\mu}(f)\le 1-\varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; \mathrm{Suc}_{\alpha\varepsilon Tk,\,\mu^{\otimes k}}(f^{\otimes k}) \le \big(2^{\alpha\varepsilon}(1-\varepsilon)\big)^k < (1-\varepsilon+0.84\,\alpha\varepsilon)^k\)
    Drucker12
    Theorem 1.1, the distributional statement everything else is derived from, for $0<\alpha\le 1$. The query budget must scale with $\varepsilon T k$ rather than $Tk$, and [Shaltiel04] shows that is essentially forced.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\text{Not with budget } Tk\text{: } \exists (f,\mu) \text{ with } \mathrm{Suc}_{T,\mu}(f) \le 1-\varepsilon \text{ but } \mathrm{Suc}_{\Theta(Tk),\,\mu^{\otimes k}}(f^{\otimes k}) \text{ large}\)
    Shaltiel04
    Shaltiel's examples: a distribution that is hard $1-\varepsilon$ of the time and trivial the rest of the time. Given $k$ copies an algorithm can hunt for the easy ones, so the success probability does not decay until the budget drops to $\Theta(\varepsilon Tk)$. This is exactly the $\varepsilon$ in Drucker's bound, and Theorem 1.1 says small $\varepsilon$ is the only obstruction.

Also in [Drucker12]: an XOR lemma (Theorem 1.3), bounding the advantage in computing $f^{\oplus k}$, and a threshold DPT (Theorems 1.4, 6.3, 6.6) bounding the probability that $\eta k$ of the $k$ instances come out right -- which decays exponentially once $\eta > 1-\varepsilon+\alpha\varepsilon$, again essentially tight by Shaltiel's examples. The threshold version is proved for total relations, not just Boolean functions, and there is a matching DPT for decision tree size (Theorem 9.1), where the resource bound grows as $T^{\alpha\varepsilon k}$ rather than linearly in $k$.

What is not known is what happens with a budget of $\alpha\,\mathrm{R}(f)k$ for $\alpha \gg 1$: see How hard is it to solve … copies?. Quantumly that regime was settled by [BNRdW07].

    Folklore: run the outer algorithm and amplify each inner call to error $1/(3\mathrm{R}(f))$, then union bound. The $\log$ comes purely from amplification, which is why $\bar{\mathrm{R}}_\varepsilon$ and the $\varepsilon$-dependence of $\mathrm{R}$ matter so much here.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n)=\Omega\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}(f)\mathrm{R}(g)}{\log(n+1)}\right)\)
    PednekarPodder26STOC
    Both f and g may be partial Boolean functions. Here n is the outer input length; replacing log(n+1) by log(R(f)+1) is not justified. Follows from Theorem 31 and the optimal outer composition theorem.
  • \(\text{FALSE in general: } \exists \text{ partial } f,g:\ \mathrm{R}(f\circ g) = O\big(\mathrm{R}(f)^{2/3}\mathrm{R}(g)^{2/3}\log^{2/3}\mathrm{R}(f)\big)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Theorem 1: the randomized composition conjecture is refuted for partial functions, by a polynomial margin. Take $f = $ \(\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k\)$_k$ and $g = \mathrm{GapMaj}_k$; then $\mathrm{R}(f) = \Theta(\sqrt{k\log k})$, $\mathrm{R}(g) = \Theta(k)$ and $\mathrm{R}(f\circ g) = \Theta(k\log k)$, against a conjectured $\tilde\Theta(k^{3/2})$. Note that both $\mathrm{R}(f)$ and $\mathrm{R}(g)$ are only logarithmic in the input size $n = k + 2^k$ of $f$, which is why the theorem with a $\log(n+1)$ loss can coexist with this counterexample.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\,\mathrm{R}(g)\big)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Theorem 3, the optimal outer composition theorem: by Lemma 6, if $\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n)=\Omega(M(f)\mathrm{R}(g))$ for all $f,g$ then $M(f) = O(\mathrm{noisyR}(f))$ -- so no measure can do better. Holds even when $f$ is a relation. The proof of optimality is one line given the characterisation $\mathrm{noisyR}(f) = \Theta(\mathrm{R}(f\circ\mathrm{GapMaj}_n)/n)$: take $g = \mathrm{GapMaj}_n$.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{fbs}(f)\,\mathrm{R}(g)\big)\)
    BDGHMT20 BenDavidBlais20composition
    Proved independently and concurrently by [BDGHMT20]; it also follows from the $\mathrm{noisyR}$ theorem above together with $\mathrm{noisyR}(f) = \Omega(\mathrm{fbs}(f))$ (Lemma 38 of [BenDavidBlais20composition]) -- see the $\mathrm{fbs}\to\mathrm{noisyR}$ record. It strictly strengthens the sensitivity version below, since $\mathrm{fbs} \ge \mathrm{s}$.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\,\sqrt{\mathrm{R}(g)}\big)\)
    GLSS19
    Holds for relational outer $f$ and partial inner $g$ -- the strongest thing that survives the relational counterexample, which rules out the full $\mathrm{R}(f)\mathrm{R}(g)$ at that generality. It is the composition-theorem form of $\bar\chi(g) = \Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{R}(g)})$.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{s}(f)\,\mathrm{R}(g)\big)\)
    GJPW18
    The generalisation of $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{AND}_n\circ g) = \Omega(n\,\mathrm{R}(g))$. Subsumed by the $\mathrm{fbs}$ and $\mathrm{noisyR}$ versions, but it was the first outer composition theorem with a nontrivial outer measure.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\,\mathrm{LR}(g)\big)\)
    BBGM22
    Optimal inner composition theorem: $\mathrm{LR}$ is the largest measure with this property.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\,\bar\chi(g)\big) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\,\mathrm{RS}(g)\big) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\,\chi(g)\big)\)
    GLSS19 BenDavidKothari18 Sanyal18 AGJKLMSS17
    The historical sequence of inner measures: $\mathrm{RS}$ [BenDavidKothari18], then $\chi$ [Sanyal18], then $\bar\chi$ [GLSS19], then $\mathrm{LR}$ [BBGM22]. Each composition theorem subsumes the previous one, but that is not the same as a pointwise chain: what is actually recorded is $\chi \le \bar\chi$ and $\bar\chi = \Omega(\mathrm{RS})$ and $\bar\chi \le \mathrm{LR} \le \mathrm{R}$. The zoo has no pairwise comparison between $\chi$ and $\mathrm{RS}$ in either direction -- do not read one off this list.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f\circ g^n) = \tilde\Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\,\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{prod}}(g)\big)\)
    Sanyal24

Status by setting.

  • Partial Boolean functions: constant-factor composition is false [BenDavidBlais20composition], but the $\log(n+1)$ lower bound is now proved [PednekarPodder26STOC].
  • Total functions: constant-factor composition is false [Meiburg26composition]; composition up to a logarithm of outer input size holds by the partial-Boolean theorem.
  • Relations: false, and this was known first. [GLSS19] give relations $f_n$ with $\mathrm{R}(f_n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$ and partial functions $g_n$ with $\mathrm{R}(g_n)=\Theta(n)$ but $\mathrm{R}(f_n\circ g_n)=\Theta(n) \ll n^{3/2}$; the outer relation is \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\) and the inner function is again \(\mathrm{GapMaj}^{\delta}_{n}\). Sanyal's theorem nevertheless allows the outer object to be a relation [Sanyal24], as does Theorem 3 above.

The earlier counterexamples -- the relational one of [GLSS19] and the partial-function one of [BenDavidBlais20composition] -- use $\mathrm{GapMaj}$ (or a close variant) as the inner function, and both work for the same reason: the outer object only needs its bits to bias $1/\sqrt m$, and buying bias $1/\sqrt m$ from a $\mathrm{GapMaj}_m$ gadget costs $1$ query rather than $m$. The total-function counterexample instead uses an encoded pointer inner function [Meiburg26composition].

Sufficient conditions for composition (all with arbitrary inner $g$).

  • $\mathrm{R}(f)=\Theta(n)$, i.e. the outer function is maximally hard [CKMPSS23].
  • $f$ symmetric, or "weakly symmetric" in the sense of [CKMPSS23].
  • Inserting a cheap buffer works unconditionally: $\mathrm{R}(f\circ h\circ g)=\Omega(\mathrm{R}(f)\mathrm{R}(h)\mathrm{R}(g))$ whenever $\mathrm{D}(h)=\Theta(\log \mathrm{R}(g))$ [BenDavidKothari18], and likewise for $h$ a parity on $O(\log n)$ bits [AGJKLMSS17].

Even a trivial outer function is not trivial. Let $\mathrm{Triv}_n$ be the promise problem on $\{0^n,1^n\}$, so $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{Triv}_n) = 1$. That $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{Triv}_n\circ g) = \Omega(\mathrm{R}(g))$ is obvious -- feed every copy the same input -- but the argument is not distributional: the hard distribution it uses is not a hard distribution for $\mathrm{Triv}_n$ composed with one for $g$, and all the composition theorems above are distributional. Getting the bound distributionally is the correlated copies problem, solved by [BDGHMT20]; here it is the special case $\mathrm{noisyR}(\mathrm{Triv}_n)=\Omega(1)$ of Lemma 37.

Sibling results for other measures. $\mathrm{D}(f\circ g)=\mathrm{D}(f)\mathrm{D}(g)$ [Savicky02, Tal13, Montanaro14], see comp-D; $\mathrm{Q}(f\circ g)=\Theta(\mathrm{Q}(f)\mathrm{Q}(g))$ [Reichardt11, LMRSS11]; $\mathrm{s}$, $\mathrm{bs}$ and $\mathrm{fbs}$ compose [Tal13, GSS16]; conical juntas compose [GoosJayram16]; direct sum dirsum-R [JainKlauckSantha10], direct product dirprod-R [Drucker12] and strong direct sum [BlaisBrody19] for $\mathrm{R}$.

Total-function counterexample. [Meiburg26composition, Theorem 1.1] gives $\mathrm{R}(f\circ g)=\Theta(\mathrm{R}(f)\mathrm{R}(g)/\log\mathrm{R}(g))$. For outer length $N$ and inner length $n$, $N=2^{\Theta(n^{4/5})}$, so the saving is $\Theta(\log n)=\Theta(\log\log L)$ in composed input length $L=Nn$. This refutes constant-factor composition and is consistent with the logarithmic-loss theorem.

The new family attains every exponent below 4, with polylogarithmic losses for each fixed k. The earlier cubic separation is retained below as a historical lower bound. Will Cook provides a great exposition and a Lean proof, with instructions for reproducing the formal checks.

  • \(\exists f \text{ total}:\ \mathrm{D}(f) = \tilde\Omega\big(\mathrm{prt}(f)^{2}\big)\)
    AKK16
    Via subcube partition complexity, $\mathrm{prt} \le \mathrm{SP}$: [AKK16] give a total $f$ with $\mathrm{D}(f) = \tilde\Omega(\mathrm{SP}(f)^2)$. This is nearly the most that can happen, since $\mathrm{D}(f) = O(\mathrm{prt}_0(f)\,\mathrm{prt}_{1/3}(f))$ [JainKlauck10, Thm 3.7].

No upper bound on $\mathrm{R}$ in terms of $\mathrm{prt}$ is known at all -- not even a polynomial one. This is the query-complexity shadow of the long-standing question of whether the partition bound characterises randomized communication complexity. What is known: for product distributions the partition bound is quadratically tight, $\mathrm{D}^{\mu}_{0.49}(f) = O\big((\mathrm{prt}_{1/8}(f)\log \mathrm{prt}_{1/8}(f))^{2}\big)$ [HarshaJainRadhakrishnan16], and for total $f$ the deterministic complexity is polynomially bounded, $\mathrm{D}(f) = O(\mathrm{prt}_{1/3}(f)^3)$ [JainKlauck10]. So any counterexample must be a partial function, or must separate $\mathrm{R}$ from $\mathrm{D}$ at the same time.
